puts a proficiency-bonus damage rider on the target Moonlight's bonus-action strike engine is already hitting, at the cost of nearly all healing above Moonlight's own Friar temp HP.

concentration-free fear off the blast routine covers the single-target lock this pairing never has, but Whisper reads 0 on sustain until its Sorcerer tail, leaving Moonlight to keep both bodies alive by mitigation alone.

Glyph.tag: rune knight wall + charisma sword-and-lore paragon
Glyph.verdict: Glyph is the rare durable body whose defensive kit runs on the clock this run actually pays for: Hill Rune's physical resistance, Cloud Rune's redirect and Runic Shield's forced reroll all refill twice per long rest, which is what a 120-supply rest cycle allows, and the Tempest opener buys heavy armour plus Wisdom and Charisma save proficiency. Spellblade covers the axes Glyph is flatly 1 on, carrying the face and the out-of-combat block on the same Charisma score that powers its sword, and Cutting Words adds a control layer that spends no concentration on a body that holds none.
Glyph.cost: Act I is thin on both halves: Glyph is one attack per Action until Act II and Spellblade's sustain is 1, so the pair's early fights are long and unforgiving. Both bodies spend slashing and fire into layered resistances, Glyph never reaches Master of Runes at 15, and Spellblade's Reckless Attack invites hits on the softer half, with Cloud Rune as the only way to move any of them.

vars.note: the best-scoring alternative at 53.5, five points below the pairing above it, and most of that gap is Spellblade's skill block walking out the door.

vars.text: Cloud Rune is the real reason Glyph is the front rank: with two Reactions per body it can redirect an attack aimed at Spellblade onto itself and still keep a reaction in hand. The armour matters less than the redirect, because the redirect is what makes Reckless Attack survivable on the other body.

Rite discipline: Crimson Rite is paid for in hit points on a body that is already the pair's damage sponge. It is worth turning on before the fights Glyph expects to redirect in, and not worth carrying through an exploration leg where the next rest is 120 supplies away.

Rime2.tag: cold-prone winter druid + maximised thunder cleric
Rime2.verdict: Two Wisdom bodies in heavy armour whose control falls out of damage they were casting anyway. From Druid 10, anything that fails a save against one of Rime2's Cold spells falls Prone, so its area control costs neither of the pair's two concentration slots, and Winter Spirit adds Wisdom to every damaging Druid spell while returning 5x Druid level in temp HP for one Wild Shape charge. TempestCleric spends the one slot the pair does hold on Spirit Guardians and stacks a maximised Shatter under it via Destructive Wrath, twice a fight off short-rest Channel Divinity. Warlock 5 puts Rime2's own slots on the same short-rest cadence.
Rime2.cost: There is no boss answer here. TempestCleric's single-target output is two attacks and a Divine Strike, well under par, and everything it does well is spread across four targets; Rime2's prone field is a save, not a lock. Out of combat both bodies are near-blind: Rime2 rolls a flat +1 Persuasion with no Perception proficiency, so any untelegraphed check has to survive that.

vars.note: swaps the second area engine for a front-rank body and Divine Guardian's halving on Rime2; the prone field stays and the maximised Shatter leaves.
the closest alternative at 54.6, and the drop is roughly what the maximised short-rest burst is worth to this chassis.

vars.text: Wild Shape as a defensive currency: Winter Spirit spends a charge to buy both the Cold rider and a temp HP bar worth five times Druid level. Against halved incoming damage that bar is effectively doubled, so the charges are better read as an HP resource than as a shapeshift.

Chapel.tag: friar bond support monk + fear-on-crit blaster
Chapel.verdict: Chapel is a support engine sized for exactly two characters: the Friar Bond ticks temp HP onto both bodies every turn, Friar's Blessing adds a d4 to every save either of them rolls, and Cleric 6 Life at character 15 adds Revivify and Disciple of Life on top of it. Whisper supplies the ranged damage and, critically, a control layer that needs no slot and no concentration, because the Bond has already claimed Chapel's only concentration slot for the whole campaign. Chains of Carceri adds a Hold Monster on the short-rest clock behind it.
Chapel.cost: The pair effectively holds one free concentration slot, not two, and its crowd answer is entirely Whisper's, since Chapel's area damage is 0 for two acts and never rises above 1. Whisper reads 0 on sustain until its Sorcerer tail, which puts the entire rescue burden on Chapel while Chapel's own Revivify does not arrive until character 15. Nothing here removes a boss's turn reliably.

vars.note: the closest alternative at 52.0, nearly five points down, which is the price of losing both the free fear layer and the ranged damage engine at once.

vars.text: The Bond is not a choice: a per-turn temp HP tick on both bodies against already-halved damage is worth a permanent concentration slot in a party of two. It does mean Spirit Guardians never appears, and that every second control effect the pair wants has to come out of Whisper's pact slots.

Riftblade.tag: warp psyker duelist + short-rest archfey blaster
Riftblade.verdict: Two Warlock-14 bodies that never touch the long-rest table. Riftblade opens a pack with Chaos Rift — one Action that Warps everything in 6 m and can hang Paralyzed, Frozen or Confusion across the whole radius — while FavoredSorcerer stands off and fires Eldritch Cone twice a round, at-will, four targets, save for half. Both casting pools refill on a short rest, so with two short rests per long rest the pair enters effectively every fight at full charge instead of dividing a long-rest table by three, and the area rows sit at 4/5/5 and 3/5/5 without either body reaching for a levelled slot.
Riftblade.cost: Rescue is 0 on both bodies in Act I and never rises above 2 on either, and Riftblade is spending its own maximum hit points every turn to Perils of the Warp with nothing in the pair that gives them back — so the drain is paid in 120-supply long rests. Durability is rung 1-2 on both, both are Charisma bodies with the same save profile, and both hold concentration, which uses the pair's entire allowance with nothing spare.

vars.note: the mirror Psyker: a second Warp detonation engine instead of a second at-will pool, which doubles the area damage and doubles the max-HP bleed with it.
trades the second blaster for a resistance-ignoring boss engine and Act III Twinned Death Ward, the only outward save cover either body would ever get.
ties this pairing exactly at 56.6, so the swap is a wash on the arithmetic; decide it on whether a second Charisma caster in light armour is a shape worth doubling.

Kinlight.verdict: Kinlight is one button held down for the whole run. Friar's Bond costs a ki, a bonus action and this body's only concentration slot, and at a party size of two it covers everyone there is: per-turn temp HP on both bodies, one chosen +1d4 on both bodies' attacks and saves, a free teleport to the partner, and a shield a Monk may wear without losing Unarmoured Defence. Beacon supplies the two things behind it — the area damage Kinlight does not have at all (0 in Act I, 1 by Act III, against Beacon's 3/5/5) and Celestial healing delivered from range while Kinlight is standing in the middle of the pack. Bladesong is what keeps that second concentration slot alive in cloth: +2 AC and +2 Constitution saves for a level tax rather than a spell.
Kinlight.cost: Both slots are permanently booked, Kinlight's by the Bond and Beacon's by whatever it is holding, so the pair can never field a third concentration effect — and Kinlight's stated want was a partner who did not need one. Neither body finishes a boss: single-target reads 2/3/2 and 2/3/3 against +170% boss hit points. Both also carry force, so one force-resistant pack shaves the Bond's damage and Beacon's blasts at the same time.

vars.note: ties this pairing at 56.4, which makes the Bond the constant and the only open question which body it is bonded to.
swaps healing at range for a heavy-armour rune toolbox that refills twice per long rest — but Glyph is 1 on skills in every act, leaving Kinlight's Lore tail to carry every check alone.

vars.text: Choose the blessing against the fight, not the build: Friar's Blessing is one blessing, not the union of four, and in a duo the choice is a party-wide buff either way. Take the save d4 in any act the pair is losing to enemy control rather than to enemy hit points.

Warpsong.tag: two psyker warlocks, one warp field
Warpsong.verdict: The maximum-Warp pairing. Every Eldritch Blast beam either body throws applies Warp and every Warp detonates for 1d10 Force in 3 m, scaling to 4d10 — so with two Actions each, four Blast actions a round land into overlapping detonations that cost no slot, no concentration and no rest clock. Riftblade's Chaos Rift at 14 then collapses a whole pack into one Warp field and can land Paralyzed, Frozen or Confusion on all of it from a single Action, which is where the pair's 5/5 area damage and 5/5 area control in Act III come from. Force and psychic are the two damage types Listo's layered resistances bother least.
Warpsong.cost: Both bodies pay Perils of the Warp out of their own maximum hit points every turn and neither one heals: rescue is 0/2/2 twice over, durability is rung 1-2, and endurance reads 2/2/3 on both. This is the 5 + 0 rule failing in the worse direction — the hole is not covered, it is duplicated, and the only thing that closes it is camp supplies.

vars.note: 54.6 against 56.4 is roughly what the pair pays to stop doubling the max-HP bleed, and it gives up the second detonation engine to do it.
the largest drop on offer at 50.5; worth it only once the run has shown that two bleeding Warlocks cannot get through Act II.

vars.text: One Psyker, one medic: nothing in this shape fixes the bleed from inside. A partner that heals every round rather than every fight is worth several rungs of area damage here, because Warp keeps detonating at full value while its caster sits at half its maximum.

Concord.tag: peace-cleric rescue chassis + hexblade curse engine
Concord.verdict: A clean division of labour. Concord holds every rescue in the pair at 5/5/4 — Emboldening Bond, Protective Bond, Balm of Peace, Revivify, Death Ward and Friar temp HP, all of it pair-scope in a party where the pair is the whole party — and Hexbind holds the entire kill rate. Hexblade's Curse adds proficiency bonus to every damage roll against the cursed target, which on a character-20 body throwing eight Eldritch Blast beams a round is worth about +48 raw per round, and it recharges on a short rest, so it is live in every fight rather than once a cycle. Protective Bond is the direct answer to Hexbind's own weakness: a light-armour caster standing in melee whenever it binds a weapon, with the tougher body able to take the hit that would drop it.
Concord.cost: Concord alone wants more concentration than the pair owns — Emboldening Bond, Protective Bond and the Friar Bond do not fit into two slots, and Hexbind is holding one of them — so something Concord was built for is always switched off. Crowd removal is thin on both sides, with Concord's area control at 1 in every act, and Concord's single-target row is 1 throughout, which makes every boss in the run Hexbind's job alone.

vars.note: the one listed swap that scores above this pairing, at 55.3 — worth pricing before the pair commits its whole output to a single cursed target.
holds no concentration at all, which hands both slots back to Concord and finally lets the Bonds run together, at the cost of the curse and several points of score.
54.6 is inside the noise; the deciding question is whether it can hold the front rank, because Concord gave up armour to be the rescue body.

Viaticum.tag: hierophant wizard rescue + order-cleric action engine
Viaticum.verdict: The utility pairing taken to its ceiling. Viaticum carries 9th-tier slots, the top of the area-control ladder and the pair's whole rescue kit on one body, and Erudite Remedy is a bonus action — so Lone Wolf's second Action is never the thing spent keeping the other half upright. Decree converts those casts into turns: Voice of Authority pays out once per ally-targeting spell, the party contains exactly one ally so it never misfires, and Embodiment of the Law casts an enchantment as a bonus action on top of that. Decree's actions row of 4/4/3 is what this pairing actually produces.
Viaticum.cost: Neither body kills anything. Viaticum is 1/2/2 on single target by design and Decree is 1 in all three acts, so a +170% boss is a fight decided by attrition and camp supplies. Worse, Voice of Authority's free attack is worth exactly what the attack it triggers is worth, and the body it triggers here is a Wizard — the pairing's headline engine is firing into the weakest weapon routine on the field.

vars.note: the Bond permanently books its own slot and leaves Viaticum's free for the 9th-tier control it exists to cast — and a Friar Monk, unlike a Wizard, is worth handing a free attack to.
the smaller of the two listed drops at 52.0; the first thing to check is whether it swings a weapon, because Voice of Authority is dead weight against anything that does not.

Gloaming.verdict: Gloaming is a reaction chassis and Lone Wolf hands every body two reactions: Ward of Shadows imposes disadvantage on an attack for free, so this one can blank two incoming attacks a round, and proportional mitigation like that does not decay against +126% enemy hit points the way a flat rider does. Rime2 supplies everything Gloaming's rung-1 damage row cannot — Winter Spirit adding Wisdom as bonus Cold damage to every damage-dealing spell and cantrip, 5x Druid level in temp HP off the same Wild Shape charge, and from Druid 10 a Prone rider on anything that fails a save against its Cold spells. That last one is rung-4 area control generated by damage it was casting anyway, so it costs neither of the pair's two slots, which is what lets Gloaming keep one for itself.
Gloaming.cost: Rime2 asked for a face and did not get one. It rolls a flat +1 Persuasion with no Perception proficiency at all, Gloaming's Lore tail reads 1/1/2 on skills, and two characters have to clear every untelegraphed check in the campaign between them. Nor does either half remove a boss permanently: single target is 1 in every act and 2 in every act, and everything Gloaming does to a single target expires.

vars.note: hands Gloaming a short-rest button that halves all damage on it for ten turns, but Moonlight is 0 on area damage in every act, so nothing left in the pair clears a crowd.
brings a Bond that covers both bodies and the Lore skills package neither of these two has — and gives up the Cold engine and its free Prone to get it.
the weakest listed swap at 50.3; nothing is worth four points here unless it reads above rung 2 on skills, which is the hole the pairing actually has.

Scourge.tag: vengeance inquisitor boss-killer + warp psyker crowd engine
Scourge.verdict: The 3 + 3 rule written out. Scourge is the single-target half at 4/4/3, and Exploit Weakness and Monster Lore both ignore resistance, which is the specific counter to a run that layers resistances on ordinary enemies rather than only on bosses — but it is 0 on area damage for two full acts. Riftblade fills exactly that gap: Chaos Rift Warps every foe in a 6 m radius and can land Paralyzed, Frozen or Confusion across all of them from one Action, taking the pair to 4/5/5 on area damage and 4/4/5 on area control. Neither body competes for the other's resources — Scourge's Channel Divinity and Riftblade's pact slots both come back on short rests.
Scourge.cost: Scourge's six Sorcerer levels arrive last, so Quickened, Twinned and the Twinned Death Ward that is the pair's only outward save cover do not exist until Act III. Until then rescue is 0 and then 2 while Riftblade spends its own maximum hit points to Perils of the Warp every turn. Both bodies also carry slashing, and both hold concentration, which is the pair's entire allowance.

vars.note: a near-wash at 54.1: the same Charisma blaster shape with no Perils bleed and a short-rest curse instead, but Chaos Rift's whole-radius Paralyze goes with it and that is the pair's only hard crowd answer.
the only listed swap above this pairing at 55.3; Scourge is 0 on area damage until Act III, so the partner's area row is what moves this number at all.

Cogtrick.verdict: The rest-free pairing: both bodies read 5 on endurance in every act and they get there by different routes. Cogtrick's contribution is permanent rather than expended — Enhanced Weapon and Enhanced Defense are flat stat on a duo that will never see four characters' worth of loot drops, and the Steel Defender is a third slot in the initiative order of a two-body party. Spellblade holds no concentration at all, so both of the pair's two slots belong to Cogtrick's Bladesinger and Arcane Trickster list, and its Bardic Inspiration runs on a short-rest clock the partner can spend on damage or healing under Magical Inspiration. Skills come out at 3/3/4 and 1/3/4, which is as close as this batch gets to two characters covering a whole campaign's checks.
Cogtrick.cost: Nobody picks anybody up: Cogtrick is 0 on rescue in all three acts and Spellblade is 1 in Act I, and the Steel Defender is soak, not a revive. Area damage is 0/1/2 against 3/3/3, the thinnest crowd row in the batch, and the pair's whole output is piercing, slashing and fire into layered resistances with no force or psychic anywhere. Reckless Attack then hands the enemy advantage against the half of the pair that has no rescue standing behind it.

vars.text: Drop the Revenant tail: Barbarian 3 arrives last and Rage is already unused because it would shut off the Spell Sword attacks, so what those three levels buy is flat DR 2 and a permanent advantage handout to the enemy. Against +126% hit points the flat reduction is worth less every act; three more Paragon or Lore levels are not.

Both slots on one caster: Spellblade holding no concentration is the quiet feature of this pairing. Cogtrick can run Haste and a second concentration effect simultaneously, which nothing else in the batch can do — build the Bladesinger's prepared list around that rather than around the scroll library.

Grimoire.verdict: Two Strength bodies in heavy armour with Crimson Rite tails, separated by clock. Grimoire is the burst half: Action Surge resets the PHB2024 War Magic counter, so a surge turn is two attacks plus a cantrip and then a levelled spell plus an attack, and Lone Wolf's second Action stacks a third pass on top. Glyph is the sustain half and is deliberately slow off the line — one attack per Action until Act II — but almost its entire toolbox refills twice per long rest, which is the only cadence a 120-supply rest actually funds: Hill Rune's physical resistance, Cloud Rune's redirect, Runic Shield's forced reroll. Glyph also covers the rescue Grimoire is at 0 on in Act I, taking the pair to 3 and then 4.
Grimoire.cost: Grimoire wanted a body to carry dialogue and Glyph is 1 on skills in every act with +0 Investigation and +0 Persuasion, so the want goes unmet and every out-of-combat check falls on Grimoire's Bard tail alone. Both bodies deal slashing and fire into layered resistances, both are Strength 22 with the same saving-throw shape and therefore the same failure mode, and Grimoire is still splitting its budget across Strength and Intelligence and behind on both.

vars.note: 58.1 against this pairing's 53.5 is the widest gap any listed swap opens; on the ledger's own arithmetic the second heavy-armour body is what is holding Grimoire down.
a real skills package and no concentration at all, which frees both slots for the Eldritch Knight — and gives up the rune toolbox and the heavy armour to get them.
at 50.3 the easiest of the three to reject; what would have to be replaced is Glyph's short-rest physical resistance, not its damage.

Pyre.verdict: These two halves are wired to each other rather than merely adjacent. Moonlight holds no concentration at all, so Pyre's one slot goes to Haste on Moonlight — a body with Martial Arts bonus-action strikes under Improved Divine Smite and a 3/4/4 single-target row against Pyre's flat 1, which is a turn genuinely worth doubling. Pyre funds its own half out of a different clock entirely: Consuming Fervor turns Fireball into a maximised 48-per-target burst and Channel Divinity is a short-rest pool, so two of them land in every fight and cover the 0 on area damage Moonlight carries in all three acts. Moonlight pays it back with Divine Guardian, a short-rest Channel Oath that halves all damage on the other character for ten turns, which is what keeps a concentrating caster's Haste standing.
Pyre.cost: The pair's entire crowd clear is fire and Moonlight has no area damage at all to fall back on, so one fire-resistant pack takes the pairing from rung 5 in Act I to nothing in a single encounter. Everything else is short-rest charges as well, Channel Divinity and Channel Oath both, so a fight that outlasts the pools is two bodies with no buttons — and Pyre's own area control falls to 1 by Act III.

vars.note: the only listed alternative and a drop to 48.9; Pyre's Haste has to land on somebody, and a partner holding its own concentration takes a slot rather than receiving one.

vars.text: Buy a second area type: the fire dependency is the one fixable thing here. Pyre's Lore tail can hold a non-fire area spell for exactly the packs that blank Fireball, and it costs a spell known rather than a level.

cards.title: The damage axes are computed
cards.body: §1 and §2 are ratios to a fixed reference body — Extra Attack, two attacks per Action, no rider, no damage feat, mundane 2d6, primary at the act's required score — multiplied by that act's enemy HP relative to Act I's. Par runs 48 / 61 / 76 on single-target and 22 / 28 / 32 on AoE. The old ladders counted features as if each were worth the same; Improved Extra Attack adds about half a body's damage and Hex adds under a tenth of it by Act III, and both used to score as one rung.

cards.title: Resources are amortised, not assumed
cards.body: Three hard fights per long-rest cycle, four rounds each. A short-rest pool refills every fight and enters at full value; a long-rest pool divides across the cycle. The action cap usually binds first — a Monk 12 holds 12 ki but two Flurries a round for four rounds spends 8. This is why a Paladin's whole smite budget amortises to less per round than one at-will rider.

cards.title: No items, anywhere
cards.body: Mundane weapons, no attunement, no Legendary. A rented capability is not a chassis property — the same objection that removed the Mirror of Loss from the Skills axis. It makes the ledger measure the build rather than the loot table, and it means Act III rungs are lower here than in v5.

cards.title: Two axes are comparable across acts
cards.body: Every other axis re-baselines per act, so a 4 in Act I and a 4 in Act III both mean 'near the best available then'. Single-target and AoE do not: their unit is pace against Act I's baseline, so a declining row is real information — the body is being outrun.

cards.title: The split is searched, not guessed
cards.body: A seed's split is one agent's hypothesis. enumerate_splits.py walks every expression each subclass can reach, composes a filter-grade vector, culls everything dominated within its (proficiency, class-set) group — 1,073,626 raw down to 88,987 — and ranks the survivors against a 5,000-body partner pool stratified across all 149 subclasses. The scoring pass then re-derives every number from the rubric.

cards.title: Fail closed, everywhere
cards.body: An unknown booster, reach, damage type or axis kind raises rather than being skipped, because a skipped effect scores as nothing and a score that is too low is indistinguishable from an honest one. This run's render refused three times before it built: missing damage types, a breadth that contradicted its own peak, and a seeds file predating a schema change.

caveats.h2: What this ledger does not know

excluded.summary: Subclasses considered and dropped, and why
items: barbarian/Path of the Battlerager — flat 1d4 spikes and 3-damage retribution that never upcast, the grapple half unshipped, and medium metal armour forfeits Unarmoured Defence.
monk/Way of the Four Elements (vanilla) — flat ki dice with no upcast path, superseded in every respect by Warrior of the Elements.
paladin/Oath of Illumination — only Aura of Brilliance is recoverable from the changelog; no level-by-level feature list is published anywhere.
sorcerer/Wretched Soul — the Nexus page carries a one-line pitch and nothing else; feature names, levels and progression are all unverified.
paladin/Oathbreaker — duplicate of Oath of Vengeance as a Charisma smite frontliner, but smites lock to Necrotic against Act II's undead.
wizard/Illusion — its best twenty-level expression is a generic full-caster body; Illusory Self is one miss per rest and nothing in the school scales.
cleric/Heavy armour table and paladin/Supporting library — a planning table and an API mod, both of which parse as subclass headings and are neither.
excluded.lead: Two subclasses the sweep first rejected as unreadable — druid/Circle of Dreams and wizard/School of Bombardment — were promoted anyway and scored on what their class text supports, with the gaps recorded per chassis.

settled.summary: Settled by reading the installed paks
items: Enemy AC is not recoverable. Character.txt declares an Armor value for only 245 of 1,548 entries and carries no Equipment field at all, so real AC lives in root-template gear. The 0.65 hit convention is therefore a stated convention, not a measurement — and it cancels between a chassis and par wherever both roll attacks.

CombatExtender's real numbers. Enemies ×2.26 HP and bosses ×2.70 by level 20, enemy AC +1 per 11 levels, boss spell save DC +1 per 7. The older '+310% / +250%' figures came from a superseded config and are roughly double the truth.

Eldritch Cone freezes at 3d10 from character 10 and its SpellSuccess never checks Agonizing Blast. It still computes as the strongest area engine in the list, because at-will four-target save-for-half twice a round outruns any once-per-fight burst; it decays 3.6× par to 3.2×, which is real but does not cross a band.
Cantrips scale on character level, not class level. A two-level Warlock dip on a character-20 body fires four full beams — roughly 0.79× single-target par from two levels.

Feats key off class level (3/6/9/12/13/15/18), so the budget is floor(A/3)+floor(B/3)+… +1 per class reaching 13. A dip is usually free, but a split where no class reaches 13 — 11/6/3, 12/8 — pays six feats rather than seven.

assumptions.summary: Assumptions that would still move numbers
items: Hit 0.65, save-fail 0.55, four AoE targets, four-round fights, three fights per long-rest cycle. These are conventions chosen so ratios stay comparable, not measurements. Moving any of them moves the whole damage column together.

AoE assumes a fixed four-target catch regardless of radius. A 3m Call Lightning and a 6m Fireball score identically. One batch scored Call Lightning at two targets on that reasoning and was re-banded to the convention for comparability; fixing it properly means banding target count by radius across every chassis.

The split search optimises the finished body, not the journey. Variants are ranked on their 20-level vector with no penalty for arriving late, so three-class splits that back-load their second and third class to characters 15–20 rank equal to ones online by character 8. The roster therefore leans back-loaded, and Act I scores across it are correspondingly thin.

Illithid powers are scored at the even share — roughly IMR 1 / 2 / 4 by act — because a row has no partner yet and only a fixed allocation keeps rows comparable. A pair sheet may concentrate the pool and lift one body at the other's expense.

Iron Mind (Gloom Stalker 7) has no representable grant in the saves registry, so both Gloom Stalker rows sit a rung light. Several other features are flagged per chassis the same way — 614 uncertainty lines across the roster.

Levelling order is not recorded. Act scores assume the level-1 class opens and the primary then runs to its breakpoint. A different order moves features between acts and would move the act columns with them.
